2/ Indiscretions with subordinates. I can even get behind the idea that Jensen is a uniquely special circumstance and we should overlook it. 

3/ Indiscretions with a potential Chinese intel asset. Let’s also fully believe the recent reporting that suggests the evidence is suspect. 

4/ Jensen as the last defense against misguided export control policy and closed lab hegemony. This is where things get tricky. But even so, let’s grant that this is a potentially existentially important counter-competitive role to play and almost no one else has the stature to do it. 

5/ At worst, he had knowledge of hardware diversion to China in violation of export controls. This is where it becomes an incredibly easy decision. Regardless of what you believe about the controls (and I believe they are both against US interests and even worse, ineffective), knowingly circumventing them is an egregious violation of shareholder and public trust. It’s also illegal. 

6/ At best, he created the perception in his affair with Alice that he was vulnerable to influence by questionable partners that could be diverting hardware to China. He can’t really change this fact regardless how true the rest of it is. It’s deeply negligent and a failure of judgment.

Paul Tudor Jones: Almost Every Big Crash Has the Same Root Cause, Too Much Leverage Somewhere

If I think of some really, really big accidents, most of them have the same underlying reason, same underlying foundation, which is some too much leverage somewhere. Most of the leverage, most of the time, if I think of the big ones, were derivative inspired, either futures or options.

1987, that crash was 100% portfolio insurance, 100%. Had they had limits, which they didn't, it would have been a 10%, maybe 15% max, but that was 100% derivatives.

If I think about 1998, Long-Term Capital, big derivatives, they had a huge balance sheet with a lot of derivatives they were offsides on.

2000 was a little different. 2000 was the easiest bear market I've ever seen in my whole life. The take that many NVIDIA supply deals were "a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract" is half right.

Jensen did made the big calls in the room. CEOs of some of NVIDIA's largest customers told me that this past week. Billion-dollar commitments, made on the spot. I'd bet suppliers saw the same. That is hard to replace.

What's overstated is the risk to the biggest deals. They're on paper.

• NVIDIA disclosed $279B in supply and capacity commitments as of July, up from $119B a quarter earlier, driven by memory. $267B of it is scheduled through fiscal 2029. You can’t report it without more than a handshake. 
• NVIDIA became TSMC's largest customer in 2025. The two biggest HBM suppliers are tightening contracts so buyers can't back out. Suppliers aren't the flight risk.
• I've said supply and the roadmap are mostly set for at least 18 months.

The real exposure is the next round: anything not on paper, and whether NVIDIA keeps committing at Jensen's pace. Rivals will bid for whatever it doesn't.

NVIDIA has a deep bench, and Colette Kress has been on calls reassuring suppliers. Tuesday's $NVDA call, her first as interim CEO, is where she shows who makes the big calls now.

en_summary: SpaceInvestor_D: $AMZN: Vulcan is fueling for Amazon Leo's first Vulcan launch, with liftoff at 12:11 PM ET today. ULA's Vulcan VC6L, with six solid boosters and a long fairing, will carry 40 Amazon Leo satellites to low Earth orbit from Cape Canaveral. It's the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has booked, after eight Atlas V missions. The window runs 12:11 to 12:40 PM ET. Amazon needs more than 3,000 satellites to finish its first constellation.

name: Space Investor
zh_summary: SpaceInvestor_D：$SPCX / $STM：三星計劃在德克薩斯州製造星鏈衛星芯片。首爾經濟日報報道三星將在其奧斯汀工廠生產 STM32V8。這是與意法半導體共同開發的 18nm FD-SOI 微控制器，SpaceX 已表示它運行星鏈的激光鏈接。三星向奧斯汀擴建投入 19 億美元，由商務部 CHIPS 補貼項目支持，目標 2030 年運營。它已在德克薩斯為特斯拉建造 AI 芯片。
en_summary: SpaceInvestor_D: $SPCX / $STM: Samsung plans to make Starlink satellite chips in Texas. The Seoul Economic Daily reports that Samsung will produce the STM32V8 at its Austin fab. It's an 18nm FD-SOI microcontroller co-developed with STMicro, and SpaceX has said it runs Starlink's laser links. Samsung is putting $1.9B into the Austin expansion, backed by a Commerce Dept CHIPS subsidy project, with operations targeted by 2030. It already builds AI chips in Texas for Tesla.
